answer: A signing key may bind only to one numbered headgate turn on a mutual irrigation ditch, and those turns are scarce: the ditch company publishes a fixed roster of cubic-foot shares that cannot be subdivided. To prove custody, the ditch-walker records a timed staff-gauge photo at the steel anchor of that gate, then matches a uniquely veined opal inlay on the paddle against a plaster cast stored with the company's founding relic minute-book. Anyone who wants another identity must buy another full water-share and occupy another gate, so the outlay grows at least linearly with each fake name.
